Every year, thousands of people assume that once they have recovered from dengue, they have little to worry about in the future. It sounds logical, but unfortunately, that is not how dengue works.Unlike many viral infections that leave behind broad protection, dengue is far more complicated. The virus exists in four different forms, known as serotypes or strains. An infection caused by one strain usually protects a person only from that specific strain, leaving the door open for infection by the other three.2/8India's first dengue vaccine: What you should knowIndia has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA (TAK-003), developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India, for people aged 4 to 60 years. Given in two doses, three months apart, the vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and does not require pre-vaccination screening. While it offers broad protection and reduces the risk of severe dengue and hospitalisation, no vaccine provides 100% immunity against every infection or strain. Experts say vaccination should be taken according to national guidelines and should complement, not replace, measures to prevent mosquito bites.3/8Dengue is not one virus, it comes in four different serotypesThe dengue virus belongs to a family called flaviviruses and exists as four distinct serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Although they are closely related, they are different enough for the immune system to recognise them separately.Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, explained, "Dengue continues to be one of the most prevalent mosquito-borne viral diseases, particularly in the monsoon months. What many are not aware of is that there are four virus strains (serotypes) of Dengue. Once infected with one strain, long-term immunity is typically only established against that one strain. They may still become infected with the remaining three strains in the future, though."This is why someone who had dengue five years ago is not automatically protected today. If another serotype is circulating in the community, a fresh infection remains possible.4/8Why a second dengue infection can sometimes be more dangerousOne of the reasons doctors take repeat dengue infections seriously is a process called antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). Scientists believe that antibodies formed during the first infection may not completely neutralise a different serotype during a later infection. Instead, they may unintentionally help the virus enter immune cells more efficiently, increasing the risk of severe disease in some people.Dr Kumar said, "As a matter of fact, dengue fever can be more serious upon a second infection with a different strain of the virus. That's why it's still the best way to avoid mosquito bites, even after experiencing dengue."This does not mean every second infection becomes severe. Many people recover completely. However, doctors recommend taking every episode of dengue seriously, regardless of whether someone has had the illness before.5/8If there are four strains, can one vaccine really protect against all of them?This is where dengue vaccination becomes more complex than vaccines for many other viral diseases.An ideal dengue vaccine needs to generate strong and balanced protection against all four serotypes. That is why dengue vaccines have undergone extensive evaluation, and different countries recommend different vaccines for different groups of people.Dr Kumar explained, "There is also a lot of debate as to whether one dengue vaccine will be sufficient to protect against all strains. The solution is not as simple as it sounds. Complete protection is required from all four strains of the dengue virus in an ideal vaccine, as incomplete protection may not be adequate."He further added, "Currently, guidelines for the use of dengue vaccines differ from country to country and are based on age, prior dengue infection, disease burden, and which vaccine is approved. Thus, vaccination should only be done after consulting a competent health expert and following the national health guidelines."6/8Even after vaccination, mosquito protection remains essentialDr Kumar said, "It is important to recognize that a vaccine is not 100% effective in eradicating the risk of dengue. Simple preventive measures are also as important."He advised, "Individuals should be protected from the bite of mosquitoes by using mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothes, using mosquito nets while sleeping, and ensuring that there is no stagnant water around the house where mosquitoes can breed."Sometimes, preventing dengue begins with something as simple as emptying a forgotten flower pot tray or covering a water storage container. These small habits can interrupt the breeding cycle of Aedes mosquitoes before they spread infection.7/8Know the warning signs, and don't wait for symptoms to worsenDengue often starts with symptoms that resemble many other viral illnesses. But timely diagnosis can make a significant difference, especially when hydration and medical monitoring are started early.Dr Kumar said, "If they start to become ill with a high fever, a very bad headache, a headache behind the eyes, joint pain, nausea, vomiting or rashes, they should go to the doctor immediately. The earlier the diagnosis, the better to prevent complications when it comes to hydration and timely medical care."He added, "Dengue can be treated successfully if recognised in time, but if not, it can worsen to a serious illness."8/8Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital.Inputs were used to explain why dengue infection does not provide protection against all virus strains, why repeat infections can still occur, and why vaccination should be taken only after consulting a qualified healthcare professional.Follow Us On Social MediaPhotostories10 traditional protein-rich dal dishes and calories per servingIndia has 5 Jantar Mantars, but only one is a UNESCO World Heritage Site; here's where they areWhy are chips packets filled with air? content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages SearchSearch All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home Taiwan News Tue, Jul 21, 2026 page4 New antibody offers possible dengue fever relief By Lee I-chia / Staff reporter Add TT as Preferred Source A research team from the National Health Research Institutes (NHRI) and National Cheng Kung University (NCKU) has identified the mechanism behind the severe inflammatory response triggered by dengue virus infection and developed a bispecific antibody that blocks it, showing promise as a treatment for dengue fever. The research team was led by NCKU Department of Medical Laboratory Science and Biotechnology professor Wang Jen-ren (王貞仁) and NHRI Immunology Research Center Distinguished Investigator Hsieh Shie-liang (謝世良). The team said an estimated 390 million dengue virus infections occur worldwide each year, with about 96 million people developing symptoms and approximately 500,000 progressing to severe disease, resulting in about 22,000 deaths annually. National Health Research Institutes president Sytwu Huey-kang, second from right, poses for a photograph with other experts during a news conference in the Ministry of Health and Welfare in Taipei yesterday. Photo: CNA In 2015, a DENV-2 dengue fever outbreak in Taiwan resulted in 43,000 confirmed cases and 228 deaths, the country’s largest dengue outbreak in decades. NHRI President Sytwu Huey-kang (司徒惠康) said at a news conference yesterday at the Ministry of Health and Welfare that dengue fever remains a public health challenge that is difficult to control. Patients might initially experience only a mild fever, but it is often followed by symptoms such as pain behind the eyes and joint pain, he said. In some cases, the condition can lead to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. There is no vaccine to effectively prevent dengue fever, and clinical treatment relies mainly on supportive care, Hsieh said. During dengue infection, activation of immune cells drives excessive production of pro-inflammatory factors, contributing to fever, he said. The pathogenesis of severe dengue is widely believed to involve dengue virus-induced overactivation of immune cells, which triggers a cytokine storm. The excessive release of cytokines increases vascular permeability, leading to plasma leakage, dengue shock syndrome and organ dysfunction, he added. Hsieh said their study confirmed that the severe inflammatory response triggered by dengue virus infection is not driven by a single immune receptor, but by the combined action of two immune receptors.The team demonstrated that simultaneously blocking CLEC5A and TLR2 can effectively suppress the excessive inflammatory response caused by dengue virus. They designed and developed a bispecific antibody capable of targeting both receptors at the same time, he said. Wang said experiments showed that the bispecific antibody reduced various inflammatory responses associated with severe dengue caused by all four major dengue virus serotypes, as well as some strains carrying mutations linked to severe disease. The team said the antibody could be a novel treatment for severe dengue fever and might have applications against Zika virus and Japanese encephalitis. The NHRI said the research findings were published this month in the Journal of Biomedical Science. Separately, the Chiayi City Government Health Bureau yesterday confirmed the city’s first imported dengue fever case, involving a student who had returned from Vietnam. The student traveled to Vietnam during summer vacation and developed fever, headache and pain behind the eyes last Wednesday before testing positive for dengue fever on Saturday, the bureau said. The bureau sprayed the area within a 100m of the victim’s home, increased mosquito density surveys and removed possible breeding sites. It advised residents to eliminate standing water and take precautions against mosquito bites, especially during dengue season.
